usual_baseline: Generic risks are almost always written; specific ones are not. Bleeding and infection near 100%, but mortality 13.2–49.2%, dislocation 0% and leg length 0% [1584][1656][2738]. Abbreviations in 54% of orthopaedic forms and 99% of surgical forms [1614][2544]. Copy offered to patients 0–12% [2613][2711][1586]. COVID-19 risk recorded 41–59% [1231][1237][2105]. Capacity documented 11.6–13.9% in arthroplasty [1257].
fix_that_works: Pre-printed or procedure-specific forms: all risks 100% [1553][2739]; risks per form 56.6% to 87.9% with stickers [1695]; uptake 91% [2008]. Electronic auto-filled forms improved most items [2317]. Emails, stickers and posters cut abbreviations 54% to 22% [1614][1395]. Teaching and posters raised copies offered 0% to 74% [2711] and next-of-kin documentation 36% to 83% [1243].
fix_that_fails: Montgomery changed nothing: 53% vs 59% of risks [2008]. Posters and induction left mortality at 21% and leg length at 6% after three cycles [1584]. Written information stayed 8–14% [1606]. Elective COVID documentation stayed poor at 48.9% [1231]. Stickers ran out and copies offered fell to 8% [1586]. New risks absent from clinic letters rose to 79% [2419].
consultant_advice: Heavily overdone, 45 audits, especially hip fracture, abbreviations and COVID risk. Teaching gives partial gains; procedure-specific or electronic forms reach near 100%. Don't audit the form again. Audit whether consent starts in clinic rather than on the day [2713][2528], whether patients get a copy and leaflet, and whether they understand the risks.
